More about the Scaleboard
The Scaleboard is a scale-only keyboard. Each key represents one note in the selected scale, with no intervening chromatic keys. The number of keys per octave equals the number of distinct notes in that scale's semitone-step recipe. Each key shows its note name and its fixed semitone index n (A4 = 0). The bold white boundary marks the currently selected tonic-to-tonic octave. The keyboard extends across the available C1–C8 range, and automatically centers on the selected octave. Select a different scale to change the key count and the spacing between the n values. Tap or hold a cyan key to hear its pitch. The Scaleboard uses the same equal-tempered tuning as the piano; only the layout changes.

MATH

Music, with the variables visible.

One coordinate system. Separate pitch, scale, harmony, and sound.

INTERACTIVE NOTEBOOK
01 Coordinates 02 Sets & circles 03 Melodies 04 String modes 05 Temperament 06 Learning map
01

Pitch is exponential. The coordinate is linear.

A4 is always n = 0. It does not move when the scale changes.

f(n) = 440 × 2 n/12
n = 12 log₂(f / 440)

The logarithm reverses the exponent: it asks, “how many octave doublings produce this frequency ratio?” A change of 12 in n doubles frequency. A change of 1 multiplies frequency by 2 1/12 .

Whole octaves + reduced remainder

m = floor(n / 12)
r = n − 12m
n/12 = m + r/12

The remainder is always 0 ≤ r < 12, then reduced. For negative n, the explicit plus sign matters: −9/12 = −1 + 1/4 , not “negative one and a quarter.”

Reducing the exponent reveals an octave subdivision. It does not turn the frequency multiplier into the same fraction: 2 1/2 = √2, not 1/2.

02

Scales are sets; degrees are positions within them.

A scale selects pitch classes. A chord selects a smaller pattern, not always inside that scale.

C major = {0, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 11}
C minor = {0, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10}

Those are offsets from C , not the absolute n values. For any tonic n₀, the notes are n = n₀ + s + 12k, with s in the scale set and integer octave shift k. The app keeps n anchored at A4.

Different numbers answer different questions

n: absolute semitone distance from A4.
Degree: position in a scale, counting its tonic as 1.
Interval name: letter span plus quality.
Chord: a root-relative interval set.

A major triad is {0,4,7}; a minor triad is {0,3,7}. “Minor” means a minor third above its root, not “outside the scale.” Sus2 and sus4 replace the third with 2 or 5 semitones.

No prohibition: scale-lock is a learning feature in Explore. Music can use chromatic notes. The tab player and chord buttons are deliberately not scale-locked.

All subsets, one-note swaps, and the circle

There are 2¹² = 4096 pitch-class subsets, including the empty set; not 4096 named scales. Seven-note subsets number C(12,7) = 792. A one-note exchange removes one included note and adds one excluded note: 7 × 5 = 35 neighbors per seven-note set. These form the Johnson graph J(12,7).

The 12 major collections form a special cycle within that network. Adjacent fifth/fourth roots share six notes, but arbitrary one-note swaps need not produce another major scale. Choosing a tonic adds information a bare set does not contain.

x → (x + d) mod 12
cycle count = gcd(d,12)
cycle length = 12 / gcd(d,12)

Other circles are constant-step root orderings, not a promise of one-note scale differences. Fourths (+5) reverse fifths (+7), because 5 ≡ −7 (mod 12).

03

A melody has both pitch intervals and time.

Exact transposition preserves semitone differences. Remapping degrees can change them.

n′ᵢ = nᵢ + t
n′ᵢ₊₁ − n′ᵢ = nᵢ₊₁ − nᵢ

The tab player applies this exact transposition to every note, then finds frets for the new pitches. Rhythm is stored separately as beat positions and durations. Whole-octave fitting is explicitly reported and can be disabled. Compact chord voicings are a separate option: they preserve chord pitch classes but may change inversions and octaves. An unplayable exact pitch is flagged, not silently folded.

Same degrees, different intervals

Degrees: 1 → 3 → 5
Major: 0 → 4 → 7
Minor: 0 → 3 → 7

A song may still be recognizable after interval changes, but this is a transformation, not exact transposition. A scale exercise conventionally starts on its tonic; a melody can start on any degree.

04

String modes are integer multiples of frequency.

Do not confuse harmonic number h with semitone index n.

f h = h f₀
y h (x,t) = A sin(hπx/L) cos(2πh f₀t)
f₀ = (1/2L) √(T/μ)

This is the ideal flexible-string model. Real strings can have inharmonic overtones due to stiffness. Every positive integer h is an allowed ideal harmonic—not just integers whose factors are 2 and 3.

Bring the harmonic back into one octave

r h = h / 2 floor(log₂ h)
octave position = log₂(r h )

The first eight harmonics reduce to four distinct ratios: 1, 3/2, 5/4, 7/4. A 6/5 minor third is the ratio between harmonics 6 and 5, not the sixth harmonic reduced by octaves.

The loudest peak may be harmonic 2 or 3. The tuner uses a periodicity estimate for the fundamental and reports the strongest FFT peak separately. Frequency alone cannot uniquely identify the physical string: different strings/frets can produce the same n.

05

Why 12? Compare the approximations.

Factorization controls symmetry. Approximation of logarithms controls tuning error.

j = round(N log₂ r)
r N = 2 j/N
error = 1200 |j/N − log₂ r| cents

One octave is 1200 cents. For the fifth, r = 3/2 and log₂(r) ≈ 0.584963. With N = 12, j = 7 and the fifth is about 1.955 cents flat. There is no universally best N: choose the ratios, weights, and cost of complexity first.

Where the targets land

Cyan ticks = N equal octave steps. Magenta lines = target ratios. Yellow dots = nearest grid step. Only this small comparison plot uses N-EDO; Explore, tabs, and the tuner remain in 12-EDO.

Compare candidate systems

All values are computed in this browser from the displayed ratios. Mean error gives every selected ratio equal weight; it is not a universal measure of musical quality or a perceptual consonance score.

What divisors really tell us—and what they do not

If M divides N, every step of M-EDO lies on the N-EDO grid. Thus 360 contains 12-, 24-, 36- and 72-EDO exactly. It does not contain 19-, 31- or 53-EDO. Refining by an integer factor cannot worsen the nearest-step error for a fixed target; an arbitrary larger grid can improve one ratio and worsen another.

For any N, the nearest-step error is at most 600/N cents. Finer grids eventually make errors small regardless of factorization. Prime N can be excellent approximations. 12 is a compact practical system, not a mathematically optimal universal winner. A complexity penalty such as mean_error + λN depends on your chosen λ.

Why a fifth never lands exactly on a finite equal-octave grid: if 2 j/N = 3/2, raising both sides to N gives 2 j+N = 3 N , impossible by prime factorization. Equal temperament approximates this ratio. Twelve pure fifths almost equal seven octaves, but overshoot by about 23.460 cents. In 12-EDO, twelve seven-semitone fifths close exactly because 12 × 7 = 7 × 12.

Other equal divisions—including 19, 24, 31 and 53—are valid mathematical designs. Musical traditions also use non-equal and context-dependent tuning; a culture should not be reduced to a single equal-division number.

06

A learning path, not a wall of terminology.

Follow the relationships from a single pitch to scales, harmony, and sound.

1. Locate a pitch

Find the same n on the piano and on two strings. Change its octave and predict the new number.

2. Change one relationship

Compare major and minor. Locate their thirds. Then move C → G and inspect the one-note scale exchange.

3. Hear time and harmony

Play an arpeggio and a block chord. Transpose a melody. Notice which intervals and rhythms stay fixed.

4. Examine the sound

Turn harmonics on. Compare sine and plucked timbres. Tune one open string, then explore different N in the tuning table.

Next layers: voice leading, harmonic function, rhythm, and form

Voice leading: changing C–E–G into C–F–A moves two voices by 1 and 2 semitones. Inversions reorder chord tones without changing their pitch classes; register and spacing still change the sound.

Harmonic function: in C major, G7 contains B and F. Their movements B→C and F→E help establish C as tonic. Membership alone does not explain the feeling of arrival. The same seven-note set can support different tonal centers or modes.

Rhythm: tempo sets beats per minute; meter groups beats; durations place sounds within that grid. Swing, articulation, dynamics and timing nuance are additional dimensions. The current player uses straight, explicitly timed beats.

Form: repetition, contrast, phrases, and larger-scale organization help listeners recognize a musical idea. Notation, ear training, counterpoint, and musical traditions beyond this model are further subjects for study.

SONGS

Practice settings

Jump to section

An octave fit moves every note together. Changing the target scale may change intervals and chord qualities; rhythm and per-note durations stay fixed. Unreachable pitches are marked ×, never silently removed.

Simultaneous notes share a vertical column. Time runs horizontally; bars and beat ticks align with duration strokes. White Δn follows the mapped melody line, not the accompaniment. Cyan = melody; magenta = chord/accompaniment notes.

One score · another key or scale

The source key and scale are the library arrangement’s stored reference, not a claim that every note is in that scale. The original score is never overwritten. Click Source · Restore to return to its original key and scale.

Change only the key: every note moves by the same number of semitones. Intervals, chromatic tones, rhythms, durations and musical roles are preserved.

Change the scale: scales of the same size map degree to degree. Chromatic source notes are fitted to the nearest source degree first. With different-sized scales, the transposed pitches fit to the nearest target-scale notes. Ties use the lower pitch. This is an arrangement, not exact transposition: some intervals, chords and unisons change. All resulting notes belong to the new scale.

Source and target: the initial target comes from Explore. You can set either target here, or choose a scale in Explore and return. A changed Explore selection is adopted on return; otherwise your Tab-page choice is kept.

Voices and harmony: cyan follows the stored melody voice; magenta follows accompaniment. Chord studies have no invented melody. When no voice metadata exists, the upper attacked note is an inferred melody path and arpeggio groups provide inferred harmony. Chord names are matched to the shared catalog after mapping; unmatched groups display their actual pitch-class names. White Δn values are recomputed from consecutive mapped melody attacks.

Playability: a whole-score octave fit may be applied. An impossible fingering is marked ×, never silently dropped; its pitch is still played. Settings provides register and exact fingering information.

Spectroscope: cyan = melody; magenta = chords; white = measured microphone audio. Audio and spectrum use the same note-role data as the score. Microphone audio is never monitored through the speakers.

GUIDE

Music, from every angle.

Explore. Choose a root and scale. Press and hold a cyan piano key or fret marker to sustain its pitch. Matching numbers identify identical pitches. Magenta outlines show chord tones; the white fretboard enclosure marks the octave shown on the piano.

Sound. Pure sine isolates one frequency. Harmonics adds upper partials to the same pitch. The sound control is shared across instruments and tab playback. Release a held note to stop it; Escape stops all playback.

Spectrum & tuner. Select a tuning, start the microphone, and pluck one open string. Auto low-cut removes low-frequency rumble. Measure room noise while the strings are muted. Analyze peaks lists measured frequencies and possible harmonic relationships. Headphones prevent reference tones feeding back into the microphone.

Tab library. Browse the alphabetical library, choose an instrument and key, and press Play. Songs, chord studies, and theory exercises share one player, including Stairway to Heaven. Δn pattern compares the original and transposed melody. Settings provides arrangement, register, reading, and loop-range controls.

Math lab. Follow the equations, compare octave divisions, and animate string modes. The pitch coordinate is always A4 = n = 0. A reduced exponent is not a frequency ratio: the ratio is 2 raised to that exponent.

Mouse, touch, and keyboard are supported. Hold Space or Enter on a note to sustain it. Pitch detection is monophonic; chords and noisy attacks can be ambiguous.

PRIVACY

Local computation. Private audio.

All audio synthesis, spectrum analysis, pitch detection, and music calculations run locally in this browser. The application uses no remote compute services, remote data sources, accounts, analytics, or advertising.

Microphone. Access requires explicit permission. Audio is analyzed in memory only: it is not recorded, saved, or uploaded. Stop mic releases access. Leaving the tuner also stops the microphone.

Browser storage. Settings and library favorites are stored locally on this device. There is no synchronization or cloud storage. Clearing the site’s browser data removes these preferences.

Website delivery. A static host serves the website’s files and may retain ordinary access logs. The app makes no API requests and sends no audio, pitch measurements, or preferences to that host. Reference links open external sites only when selected.

Seven modes · same collection, different tonic

A tonic is a perceived center, not just the first note you play. Phrasing, bass and harmony help establish it. Reinterpreting the same melody can preserve every Δn while changing its scale-degree meaning.

Minor forms & other collections

Natural, harmonic and melodic minor describe useful collections within minor-key practice—not three mandatory, separate kinds of key. Harmonic minor raises degree 7; melodic minor ascending raises 6 and 7. The classical descending form usually uses natural minor; jazz commonly retains the ascending collection both ways.

The scale selector also includes pentatonic, six-note blues, whole-tone, octatonic and chromatic collections. These are not all the world's musical systems; this lab uses twelve-tone equal temperament.

Each line is aligned to its own first melody note. Equal shapes mean equal melodic gaps—not necessarily equal chord voicings. The invariant check above includes every recorded voice. Preview: first 16 beats.

Inspect the arithmetic · source n, degree, target n & Δn

Signed integer n is relative to A4 = 0. R and R′ are tonic references in a chosen octave. d is a zero-based position in a seven-note scale; o is the octave displacement from its tonic.

Creates an unsaved study. The original library entry stays unchanged.
A scale is a palette around a tonic. A chord is a simultaneous pitch recipe around a root. A chord can include notes outside the selected scale.

Chords built from the selected scale

Take alternating scale positions: 1–3–5 (–7). Lowercase numerals indicate a minor third, ° diminished, + augmented, ø half-diminished. Degree numbers refer to this scale; ♭III-style major-reference notation is not used here.

One chord, two independent choices

Magenta marks chord tones outside the source scale. These still sound through chord playback. Changing an inversion changes the exact voicing, not the chord's pitch-class collection.

Chord dictionary · thirds, sus, 6, 7, add9 and extensions

These are explicit teaching voicings. Real 9/11/13 chords often omit or alter tones. “Sus” replaces the third in a basic sus2/sus4 chord; it does not mean “sustain” and it is not a key type. A sustain pedal changes duration, not chord membership.

Hear how context changes the meaning

Scope & reference reading

The exact n model describes pitches and recorded timing in twelve-tone equal temperament. It does not claim that a scale set determines a key, that every song has one fixed key, or that any collection dictates which notes are allowed. Context, register, timbre and musical tradition matter. Scale-degree conversion is an explicit compositional transformation, not a unique way to convert every chromatic song.

About the pitch coordinates grid

old deg shows degrees in the previously selected scale, and new deg shows degrees in the current scale. Blank cells mean that pitch is not part of that scale. Changing the octave shifts both rows together.

old deg and new deg identify scale degrees before and after the change. note gives its pitch name and octave. n counts semitones from A4 = 0 and is informational only. Click or hold a cyan or magenta note cell to play that pitch.

n/12 is the octave exponent in f(n) = 440 × 2n/12. It is displayed as floor(n/12) + remainder/12, with the remainder unreduced and between 0 and 11. The fraction is shown on the next line.

Colors: cyan marks scale tones; magenta marks tones in the selected chord. A white outline follows each sounding note on the grid and its corresponding instrument position during playback.

On narrow screens, swipe the grid horizontally to see all thirteen semitone positions, including the upper tonic. Octave controls move the displayed register without changing the selected scale.
